I do not purpose taking up a great deal of the time of the committee this afternoon, but there are a few things which I should like to say concerning this proposal of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to spend another 820,000,000 of the people's money upon building and, after building, operating a national system of steamships. There is an argument for nationalization of railways. It has been noted by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) that where anything is a monopoly, either natural or quasi-natural, it is proper and right that that should be controlled by the community. There is, in that sense, an argument which largely offsets, although perhaps it does not altogether offset, the loss of efficiency in management which nearly always goes With bureaucratic or Government control as opposed to individual or company control. But that argument which applies to the nationalization of railways has no application at all in connection with the operation of tramp steamers. That is what these steamers "will bo; they are not of. the size to be used as large transatlantic or transpacific liners; they are the size of vessels which are engaged as tramp steamers, the sort of steamers which have built up in no small measure the wonderful mercantile supremacy of the Old Land. I cannot conceive of any business more inapt, if I may use that word, more improper for Government or bureaucratic control than the management of tramp steamers. You have to be able to watch the trade routes of the world, to bring your vessel home from Buenos Aires and on the next voyage send it off to the Black sea. I cannot understand how a Government can properly manage tramp steamers. The hon. member for Red Deer has very properly stressed the absurdity of a protectionist Government such as this Government is, endeavouring with a tariff to keep goods out of Canada and at the same time to build up international commerce by lines of steamers. But that is not the point I wish to make this afternoon, as it has been very well made by the hon. nrember for Red Deer. The point I want to make is the impropriety and unwisdom of the Government as opposed to individual or company endeavouring to operate ships. I remember during the war consulting a very well known steamship man of Montreal as to the efficiency which the British Government obtained from the British ships which, as a war measure, they had taken over. The British Government, in order to have the preference of the service of their 
mercantile marine, laid hands on the mercantile marine of Great Britain. I was told by this friend of mine that the ships were not operated above 60 per cent efficiency, because why? Not because the men who operated them were not patriotic, not because they were not trying to do their very best, but because they did not have the necessary information and freedom, the necessary initiative to carry on the operation of managing ships as private individuals or those in the employ of a company would have had. That is, to my mind, the great and fundamental objection to this scheme of the nationalization or the establishment of a national system of ocean-going vessels. We have had mixed up with the excellent and lucid exposition of the minister, paeans of praise of the protective system raised by hon. members on the other side. The hon. member for Toronto Centre (Mr. Bristol), who rarely visits this Chamber, has given us the benefit of an excellent speech in support of the principle of protection. May I remind him of a story told by some Portuguese legislator? There was a proposition made that the Tagus should be widened and deepened and made suitable for the conduct of commerce up and down that river in order to foster trade between Portugal and Spain; but Portugal had at 'that time a high tariff against Spain, and this Portuguese legislator said: " How ridiculous it is for us to endeavour to keep Spanish goods out of Portugal with a tariff and then to spend money on deepening the Tagus ! Let the Tagus run to the sea as it did in the time of our forefathers." But it is the impropriety and unwisdom of placing the control of tramp steamers in the hands of a bureau, of a Government department, against which I wish to protest-. The minister is in the happy position of being able to get out of this business with a profit. Let him embrace the opportunity at the earliest possible moment. Then he will have deserved well of his country; he will have entered into stupendous financial operations and closed those without a loss. How rarely in the history of this country have large operations of a quasicommercial or industrial character been entered into by a Government and abandoned by the Government without loss!
I press this upon the minister. I am glad that he has made money with his ships and I shall be still more glad to see the exact figures w'hen he lays them before the House, but now that he has made a profit let him remember the French proverb which says that " the better is the enemy

of the good." Let him be satisfied to call a halt and bring -these operations to a conclusion when he can do so without loss to the state.
Mr. JOHN H. BURNHAM: Mr. Speaker, I think a casual listener to this debate might get the impression that a large number of the members of this House had been sent here by private interests in order that they might thoroughly smash up everything they possibly can that is in the public interest. They do not seem to be pleading for the public interest. They try to show that it is utterly and absolutely impossible to conduct public business, and that it ought to be left to private individuals. If that is so, why do not these- gentlemen leave this Chamber and go home, leaving the affairs of this country to private individuals? Simply because it is impossible to carry on the public business of this country in that way. The answer is before these gentlemen if they will only notice the things that are so plain. Will my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) for one moment contend that public efficiency is so inferior to private efficiency that the Government of Canada should have handed over to a private company the prosecution of the war? There seems to be no discrimination at all in these matters. Let us be patriotic; let us be sensible, and remember that we are here to transact the public business in a public way and by public means, and that it is not to be left to private individuals.
Do not let us forget that it is but a few years since we were at the mercy of the Atlantic shipping pool, and God forbid that we should ever be at the mercy of another shipping pool in our time. If the Minister does not go on with his public ownership programme in the matter of shipbuilding, and give the industrious farmers and labour generally throughout this country a fair show on the ocean, as it has agreed to give to them on land, the Government will certainly meet with the strong disapproval of the people of this country.'. We do not want the main lines of communication in the hands of private individuals.
Lest the observations of that scientific reasoner the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) go without challenge, I should like to devote just two minutes to his observations. First of all, he said British shipbuilders, because of free trade, had driven American shipbuilders off the sea. That I absolutely deny. If the hon. gentleman will read the latest work on the history and development of the American
marine and American shipbuilding, he will find that from the time American shipbuilding began, British shipbuilders, Norwegian shipbuilders, French shipbuilders, and shipbuilders of every other nation were wiped off the sea by the Americans. It was the Americans with their old clippers who had the lines of shipping to Canton, South Africa, South America and Europe, and one very interesting thing in connection with those clippers is this: It was not the sharp bow that gave speed and efficiency but the blunt bow, which gave both capacity and speed. This history is one of the most interesting things in the world to review. You will find that the Americans simply captured the trade of the oceans. Then what happened? Under protection the American republic developed scr rapidly that it looked about for other nations to do its bidding, to do its hewing of wood and carrying of water, its carrying on water, and when the Americans -were asked why their shipbuilding had not been proceeded with and why Great Butain had been allowed to monopolize the shipping business they said: " It is because we have so much else to do. We prefer to let Britain do it, and to hire her ships." There are vast numbers of ships which the British shipyards are credited with building, and duly and properly credited with which, however, are under American registry. Tne Americans will build ships only as soon as they need to do so; it is not that they cannot build them, or because the system of protection forbids it. In the meantime they are drawing from the United Kingdom, Canada, and from all parts of the world, shipping and everything conceivable to enable them to expand as they are doing. Do not let anybody run away with the idea that our shipbuilding is not equal to that of Great Britain because we are said to have a false fiscal system in this country. That is not so at all. You cannot compare Canada with Great Britain, although the minister has announced to-day what has been achieved, and that we are able to take contracts on an even keel, as it were, even with the Old Country itself. That augurs well for the future, if we have a good governmental system. The trial spin has shown what we can do.
There is. an extraordinary kink, as it were, in the free trader's mind. Having enunciated the general principle of absolute freedom of trade, he seems to be utterly unable to understand that other elements enter in. Let me illustrate. If between the hon. member for Brome and myself there

should spring up a syatem of trade it follows, as the night the day, that if my labour cost is equal- to his and his to mine, then absolute free trade must obtain between us. But if-and here is the point-I make a profit as against the hon. member for Brome I take just that much away from him and do not give him any return for it. If I make a 25 per cent profit, I do 75 per cent of the work and he does 100 per cent; he is 25 per cent behind. If I make 50 per cent profit,. I only do half the work, and if I make 75 per cent profit, I do only .one-quarter of the work and to that extent make no exchange of work. This element of profit, which is the basis on wdiich all modern commerce is conducted is absolutely and entirely left out of consideration by these gentlemen. Profit is the basis on which all commerce is founded, and we surely have a clear example of that in the exchange situation to-day, when the United States is making us pay through the nose. It is absurd to say that Great Britain has been able to capture the ' commerce of the seas by reason of her free trade policy, and that because she exports she must import, because^any one acquainted with the facts knows that half the time British shiping goes home absolutely empty. It is no good my hon. friend (Mr. Mc-Master) shaking his head, because that is a fact. Her profit and her subsidies enable her to do that.

Can the hon. member give us the figures?
Mr. BURNHAMI can give the figures but I am laying down now simply a general principle. Let me tell the hon. gentleman, whether he likes it or not, that in order to prevent any loss whatever the British Government subsidizes these lines, and it is this policy that enables Britain to maintain the monopoly of the sea. If I had a telegraph line and discovered that I could lose on telegraphs and make a profit on something else I would be content to lose on telegraphs, and the hon. member for Brome would exclaim: " There, look at what free trade will do"; whereas, as a matter of fact, I am making on something else. It is the same way with the British Government. They know that, from their insular position, if they do not carry the trade of the nations they are undone. They therefore build ships and subsidize them, and in that way get the trade of the world.
Does my hon. friend mean to say that the British Government subsidizes tramp or freight steamers?

It subsidizes whole
lines; not all, I admit, but it subsidizes lines, and especially missionary lines; and when these missionary lines have run the others out, then perhaps they withdraw the subsidies, as they have sometimes done. But read the history of the development of the American marine and you will find it all laid down there, and you will discover that your antiquated ideas are like cobwebs in your brain. Sweep them out; they are not true; they are not correct; they are not founded on common sense; and business is founded on common sense. Do not, when you are discussing general principles, omit some of the other principles that bear directly on them. You might just as well calculate the orbit of the' moon without taking into consideration the influences of the planets and of the sun. Some of the earlier astronomers did that and could not understand why they were wrong. After Newton discovered the law of gravitation, when they made calculations without considering other heavenly bodies, they found that they did not work out. For example, when Herschell discovered Uranus a calculation being made of the orbit of that planet, it was found that it was more than 200 miles out. This appeared to be a negation of the Newtonian theory, but a young Frenchman, Leverier by name, made a calculation on the supposition that the Newtonian theory was correct, namely, that the influence of a planet still further out would account for the unusual motion of Uranus; and, proceeding on' that assumption, he discovered Neptune.
Now let me commend this sublime illustration, this tremendous example, as something that may possibly attract the attention of the hon. member for Brome when he is discussing the law of free trade. Let him remember that there are countless other things that pull and haul it in other directions, and until he has taken those into consideration his calculations are absolutely wrong.

' I rise to ask a question of the minister. Early in March I asked the following question, as appears in Hansard on page 327:
* .
1.	How many contracts for shipbuilding were given by the Government since the 1st of January, 1918?
2.	To what firms were said contracts given and what were the respective amounts?
The answer was that there were fifty-six contracts given, and the minister this afternoon in his speech stated that they were

given for the sum of $43,704,962.13. In answer to the following question:
Were all of said contracts given after tender?
The following information was given:
Contracts were placed after orders had been received from the several yards and prices and other details agreed upon.
My fourth question was:	" If so, were
they given by the lowest tenderer?" and the answer was, " Answered by number three." The answer to my fifth question, which was:
If not, why?" was " Answered by number three."
I have listened very carefully to the speech of the minister this afternoon and I am rot very clear yet as to whether these conti icts were given to the different shipbuilding companies after proper tenders had been made. Was an opportunity given to 2very shipbuilding company of Canada to tender?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The policy of the
Government., when it was inaugurated in 1918, was to keep busy the existing yards then located and operated in Canada. In addition to these yards that were in existence at the time the policy was announced, two or three new yards have been established. We did not advertise for public tenders in the way suggested by my hon. friend, for the reason that if we did one or more yards might get too great a share of the business. The policy of the Government was to distribute the business evenly in order to keep all of the yards busy and give employment to the workpien in various parts of the country, and, after the Armistice was signed, to returned soldiers. Every yard in Canada was therefore asked to bid for the Government's business. As I stated this afternoon, our own experienced technical officers figured up the cost, so that we had a check on the prices that were submitted to us by the various yards. We also had the Old Country costs to go by. We carried on negotiations for certain types of ships with various yards, making as .good a business deal as possible. As I say, we could not call for public tenders in the usual way, because some yards might not get any business while others might obtain too much. As I explained to the House this afternoon, the average cost of Canadian government ships is less than the American cost, and less than the cost of ships ordered by the Imperial Munitions Board.
There was no competition?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the Government desired to place a contract for two or four ships of, say, 8,400 tons, such ships could not be built on the Lakes, and we would ask shipbuilding concerns on the Pacific coast, and at Montreal, Three Rivers and Halifax to give prices for these ships, and *we would make as close a bargain as possible, first of all having the cost of the ships ourselves, then having the bids from the yards capable of constructing ships of this, size, and having other information to .guide us. Altogether, I think we safeguarded the public interest as effectively as if we advertised for tenders in the usual way.
Does the minister not think that if tenders had been called for in the usual way the Government would have been able to secure lower prices?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
In regard to the manning and officering of these ships, has the minister been able to procure Canadian seamen and officers, or have we had to bring outsiders into the service?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: While the ships are owned by the Government, they are not directly operated, by the Government. The Canadian Gover'nment Merchant Marine, the stock of which is owned by the Government. is entirely under the management of Mr. Hanna and his board of directors, and tlie organization which he has for the operation of ships. I have_no direct knowledge of the personnel of the crews; the Canadian Government Merchant Marine look after that matter as well as the operating of the ships. Incidentally, I might say that I asked Mr. Hanna some time ago if they were many Canadians and he said " No." As a rule the majority of the crews for the time being are old countrymen, but Mr. Hanna gives the preference wherever Canadians are available. My department is doing everything it possibly can, with its schools of navigation throughout the country, to iAduce Canadians to take the necessary course to become officers or engineers, deckmen and so on. I hope that in the future the majority of the crews will be Canadians, but at the present time they are hot.	*
We had a discussion a few days ago as to whether or not we had commanding officers available, and I .had that in my mind when I asked the question.

The minister spoke about the cost of Canadian ships in comparison with those built in other countries. This after-

1

noon he gave us figures of contracts made in Great Britain in comparison with those made in Canada. Does he figure the cost in pounds or dollars, and does he take the English pound as having a value in Canadian currency of 4.86 2/3, or what rate of exchange does he take at getting at the figures?
Mr. BiALLANTYNE: I did not do the figuring myself, and I would not want to give an answer to the hon. member for Lunenburg unless I knew that the figures were absolutely authentic. I will ascertain and let the hon. gentleman know.

Mr. Chairman, the debate
which took place this afternoon was a very interesting one, but apart from that, it appealed to us of tire Liberal Party, inasmuch [DOT] as it reminded us of another which took place some ten years ago, when the leader of the Liberal Party suggested that we should build in this country a Canadian navy which would promote a new industry, that of shipbuilding, and would certainly lead later on to the building and maintenance of a fleet of merchantmen.
At that time, the leader of the Liberal Party, represented in the House of Commons and throughout the country, the thoughts and ideals of. all true Liberals of the day. If I remember well, the present Minister of Marine, who was then a member of the Montreal Board of Harbour Commissioners, was among the strongest and most enthusiastic supporters of such .policy.
It is useless, Sir, to revert to the past; it i,s useless for us, on this side of the House, to recall the debates, the bitterness of which, however, is not quite forgotten. As I said before, if I remember well, the very man who led the forces opposed to that policy is today leading the Government in this House- I refer to the Right Hon. Acting Prime Minister. If you cared, Mr. Speaker, to read over again the discussions which took place at the time, you would be very much surprised to notice that the same man whose Government now propose an expenditure oi $20,000,000 for the building 'of a Canadian merchantmen was the first one in the IJouse of Commons and throughout the country, to raise his voicd against .such a policy and to oppose Laurier's "tin-pot navy." We read in the Gospel that there. shall be joy in Heaven upon [DOT] one sinner that doeth penance, more than upon ninety-nine just who need not penance.
To-day, Sir, as a member of the Liberal Opposition in this House, as a representa-

five of the people who entered the field in 1911 as a supporter of the naval policy oi Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and wa;s defeated, it is a matter of gratification to me to congratulate the Right Hon. Acting Prime Minister and to tell him that I hope that his change of heart, however, late it may be, will prove genuine. And to guote again the Gospel, knowing as I do that the Acting Prime Minister is quite conversant with it, let me tell him that according to Holy Scriptures, the best rewarded labourers were those who came about the eleventh hour.
I do not wish, Sir, to discuss the question on its merits, whether Canada should [DOT] have a Canadian merchant marine or whether we are entitled to have ships flying our national flag; for to such a question there can be but one answer. Yet, I think there arises an incidental question and I anticipate much trouble in the future, unless the Government tackle the problem and immediately solve it. The man who deals with the upbuilding of this new merchant marine with its operation and in a general way with its development, that gentleman,
I say, is Mr. Hanna, of the C.N.R. Now. Sir, I 'say that if the Government of this country want to be fair and deal honestly with the Canadian ratepayers, and if the Minister of Marine wants to be consistent, and to live up to his Liberal principles-as I have no doubt he should-act-
I say that the hon. minister has but one thing to do and it is this: Let him dismiss Mr. Hanna and all those who in any way, are connected with the C. N. R. Here are gentlemen who have fleeced the country, here are men who have bled white nearly each province of Canada; here are men who after 'building throughout ithe country railway lines in an, extravagant and irrational way, have extorted from a too liberal and obliging Government millions which are now filling the coffers of promoters such as Mackenzie and Mann. The thieves must be cast out of the temple, whether that temple be the Government of Canada or the House of Commons. The Hon. Minister of Marine has an Imperative duty to discharge: Let him take up his whip, like an honest man, and exipel all the knaves from his department,
Is the Government Warranted in givin away another $20,000,000, and in handin that money over to that man Hanna who has brought ruin to the Northern Canadian and extorted from the public treasury hun-reds and hundreds of millions, the wherewithal to pay the debts of unscrupulous financiers^
fcf; tfj

One more remark and I am through. Formerly the city of Quebec was the centre of the shipbuilding industry in Canada. The hon. member from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) who always gives proof of erudition and is anxious to be looked upon as a scholar by his colleagues, has just referred to a new shipbuilding policy. Let me tell my hon. friend that he came over to Canada rather too late and that had he come to this continent a little earlier he would know that the shipbuilding business was thriving in Canada in the early sixties and seventies, down to 1875, and this because of an .imperative necessity, as civil war was waging in the United States of America, and the Americans were having a very large number of ships built in this country. Whether success is attained in shipbuilding or not, it does not depend upon the fiscal policy, but upon favourable opportunities.
Sir, my opinion on the whole shipbuilding policy is very simple, and in fact so simple that it should also be shared in by the hon. Minister of Marine. I stood in 1911 on the same ground as Sir Wilfrid Laurier did, and the hon. Minister of Marine also took the same stand. Now, in 1920, I stand for the same policy and the members of the Government seem to hold the same views. In connection with this policy, let the hon. Minister of Marine recall that he was a follower of Sir Wilfrid Laurier; let him be mindful of the principles which he then advocated, and so doing he will ever protect Canadian autonomy. Let him not forget the dangers that threatened our trade during the war, because of the fact that England wanted to take over all our Canadian ships and let him in the future see to it that England be mistress in her own house, so far as marine is concerned, and Canada mistress in her own home.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is now six o'clock
and I leave the chair.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.
House again in Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the House rose at six o'clock we were considering Item 219, providing for the Government shipbuilding programme, in the Main Estimates for the year ending March 31, 1921. The item had been under consideration since three o'clock and had been fully discussed. Is it the 411
pleasure of the committee to adopt the resolution?

We are asked to vote the
large sum of $20,000,000 to carry out the Government's shipbuilding programme, but we are not given a very lucid explanation of the reasons for that expenditure. We are' greatly indebted to the minister for presenting to us the information he had in regard to the item, but I was somewhat disappointed and rather surprised when he said in answer to an hon. gentleman that he did not know whether the information he was giving was correct or not because it,had not been prepared by him.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I might say to the hon. gentleman that every figure I gave this afternoon I prepared personally with the exception of the sterling cost of the ships.

I was not referring to the
statement of my hon. friend but to his reply in answer to a question. Doubtless the minister's statement was correct in so far as it went; but it seems to me that in asking for such a large amount of money at any time, and particularly under present conditions, he should be prepared to give further and detailed explanations in regard to this item. The minister somewhat hurriedly gave a list of ships that had been built, and other details the effect of which it was difficult to grasp without a little study. I would like to know whether the contracts for these ships were let by public tender, and if so whether the lowest tenders-were accepted. Or are the ships being built under force contract, with provision for a certain percentage of profit? These are matters of detail which the minister. should place before the committee before we are asked to vote this large amount of money.
I do not intend to discuss the question of what should be a proper policy in the matter of shipbuilding. I am free to say that I am not in a position to know whether a policy of shipbuilding by the Government is the best thing for the country. Of course, I have my own opinion about it, and I suppose -all other hon. members have theirs ; though, their opinions may be based upon more knowledge- of -the matter than I possess. But the advisability of building merchant vessels at the present time is very , questionable. It is questionable whether the minister did the right thing when he went into the building of a merchant marine a year or two ago-at a time when the cost

of construction was very greatly enhanced. The minister said this afternoon that notwithstanding the huge expenditures that had been made in the building of these vessels, the return as a result of operation was on the right side. But have the expenditures connected with the operation of these vessels been charged up to the proper accounts, or have they been charged up to the operation of the Canadian National railways? Has a portion of the salaries of the directors of the Canadian National Railway system been charged up to the earnings of the vessels whose operations my hon. friend says have .paid a dividend? We cannot know that there has been a proper return on the *expenditure made or that there has been a net profit on operation unless we know that these things have been properly charged against the, operations of the different vessels. Generally speaking, having regard to the experience of the past, we cannot, in the operation of steamships by a Board ol Management appointed by the Government, expect to meet with the greatest financial success. When my hon. friend gives a glowing account of the results which have been achieved through the operation of the Government vessels, he must realize that in the years to come freight rates will not be [DOT]as excessively high as they are now, and that he is building his vessels at a time when costs and charges are at almost the highest possible point. I think it was the member for Toronto Centre (Mr. Bristol) who said-the minister hinrself also said it -that we could sell these vessels to-day at ,a< profit. If he can dispose of them at a profit, I would suggest that he do so, for two reasons: First, the responsibility of financing -the undertaking would be removed from the shoulders of this country; and, second, the chance of loss in operation would be done away with so far as the country is concerned. Besides, if we handed these vessels over to private interests, we would not then be interfering with or competing with private individuals who were prepared to go into the shipping business. If, therefore, my hon. friend can transfer these ships and rid the country of further responsibility in regard to them without subjecting the country to any loss it is my opinion that he should do so.
Is the Board of Management which has charge of the operation of these vessels a member of the Shipping Federation of Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I cannot make a positive statement, but I should judge that

they would be. That, however, in no way binds them as to freight rates.
What are the functions ol the Shipping Federation of Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am not familial
with the functions of that body, but I should judge that they would deal with pilotage matters, aids to navigation, harbour dues, allocation of berths and so on. But they have nothing whatever to do with the fixing of rates.
Will the minister say that the government-owned ships are competing with other lines running into Canadian ports?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Certainly.
Are the government-owned ships charging lower rates?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am not familial
with the rates charged by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine but naturally they would meet competition where necessary. I cannot say whether or not their rates are lower.

As I understand it, one
of the principal reasons for the building and operation of this Canadian Merchant Marine was that we might be able to ship our products overseas at a lower rate. Unless the Canadian Merchant Marine by competition decreases the cost of transporting freight I hardly see that there is much reason for its existence now that the war is over. It is essential that the minister assure the House that by means of the merchant marine built by the country we shall be able to ship our products overseas at a much better rate than heretofore. If the minister will not answer in regard to this matter, he may answer me in regard to something else. Were any arrangements made with the British Admiralty regarding the taking over of Canadian Government ships during the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The British Minister of Shipping had no authority to take over ships of Canadian registry during the war without the consent of the Canadian Government. As to ships under British registry, he had the right to commandeer without consulting the Canadian Government.	_

Is it not a fact that tons of freight were lying on [DOT] the wharves at Montreal and that we were unable to send it overseas because the British Admiralty

had taken all space for freight going from Canadian ports during the latter days of the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: On ships under British register the British Minister of Shipping commandeered 70 per cent of the available cargo space. As regards ships under Canadian register, such as the Canadian Mercantile Marine, he had no such authority, and did not exercise any.
Was the available space on the Canadian Government Merchant Marine given one hundred per cent to individual shippers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
None given over to British Admiralty purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not an ounce.
Could the minister tell us where he expects to get this amount of $20,000,000 from that he purposes spending on shipping?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the hon. member will ask that question of my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), when the Budget is brought down, I am sure he will tell my hon. friend. In a general way we shall get it from the revenue of the country, and if that is not sufficient, I suppose, maybe, it will be necessary for the Government to depend on the banks. But I think that question should more properly be put to my colleague the Minister of Finance.
But the question is before us now to deal with as to where this money is to come from.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that we shall get the money.

This is a matter in which the Canadian people are interested. The time has come when the people of Canada are about tired of spending borrowed money for the promotion of the industries of this country. At the last session of Parliament we had the Minister of Finance borrowing money from the Canadian people in order to lend it to countries so that they could buy goods from this country with that money. Much of that money-	'

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I regret very much to be obliged to call the hon. member to order, but I must remind him that the House is now sitting as a Committee of Supply and not as a Committee of Ways
and Means. The finding of moneys for all purposes mentioned in the Estimates comes properly before the committee when it is sitting as a Committee of Ways and Means.

I just wanted to point out by way ojf illustration that we had been spending a great deal of money on various things for the promotion of the rich men's interests in this country, and this apparently is one of them. This is not only a question of where the money is to come from; it is a question of the policy of the Government. The very item itself states that it is to complete or to promote the Government shipbuilding programme. If the Government have a programme, it must necessarily follow that they have a programme for providing the money for this shipbuilding, and I am simply asking the Government how they purpose going- on, if they intend to go on.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I must again point out to the hon. member that the question of where the money will come from or how the money will be provided is not in order at the present time.
Mr.. CAHILL: I just want to bring to the attention of the Government the absurdity of their going on spending money by the millions when they do not have it. It is necessary to make some reference to expenditure in order to bring out the point that I wish to illustrate. The Government are spending money on every hand by the millions-
By the hundreds ot millions.

-by the hundreds- of millions, and they state that this vote is to carry out a policy. What I wish to know is where this policy is to lead the country, where the people of Canada are coming to with this policy. We were told this afternoon by one of the supporters of this Government that we must go into the shipbuilding business now in order to provide traffic for the railways. Where is. the thing to end. The hon. member who made that reference also stated that we must expect deficits which will come out of the pockets of the people of Canada. I merely want to know from the minister if there is any end to the ambitions of the Government to spend the money of the Canadian people for the benefit of the friends of the Government.	[DOT]

The minister has been asked with regard to the amount which appears

in the Estimates in connection with the shipbuilding programme. It seems very strange to me that a business man should ask his shareholders to approve an expenditure of $20,000,000, or of any amount, without knowing where the money is to come from when he asks for it. It seems to me that the first thing that we should know, whether it is in' ordei or not, is where the money is coming from. No Minister of the Crown should come before this committee without being able to give the information as to where the money is to come from before he asks for it.
I should like to know from the minister how these vessels are chartered. The hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) asked whether the freight rates were higher or lower than the ordinary dealers' freight rates. Are these vessels chartered through brokers or directly through the agents of the Mercantile Marine Corporation?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The vessels are not chartered at all. There is more freight offering both for the outward voyages and the inward voyages than the vessels are able to carry. There is no necessity to charter them in view of the large quantity of freight constantly offering.
Does the minister refer to Canadian freight or foreign?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Mostly Canadian.

That is not an answer to my question. I do not care whether there is ten times as much freight offering as can be carried. The fact that a vessel carries freight means that it is chartered; that is, a merchant in Quebec, Montreal or Toronto must charter space in a vessel to carry freight; and I would like a direct answer to my question.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I thought I had made the matter clear to the hon. mem-her who is a shipping man. The Canadian Government Mercantile Marine do not * charter their vessels; they see to it that there is an abundance of freight for them. Their vessels are handled the same as the Canadian Pacific or the White Star or the Cunard handle their vessels. Vessels are not chartered through brokers at all. The freight is sent to whatever port the ship is going to sail from, by the Government, railways or by some other railway, and the Canadian Government Mercantile Marine sees to it that the freight is there when the ship is ready to sail; but they certainly do not charter any of their vessels.

The last answer is what .I wanted. The vessels are chartered. The trouble is that the minister does not know what the word " charter " means. A vessel is chartered by John Brown of Montreal or John Jones of Toronto to carry 100 casks of rum from Montreal:-
Oh, oh.

-or flour or anything else. I am pleased at the sentiment that emanates from the other side. Last year I noticed that when the vote was about to be taken many members absented themselves because they did not want to vote for prohibition. I am glad to know from the minister that these vessels are chartered without commissions being paid. Do these vessels pay a business profits tax to the Government? Every private ship owner in the country has to pay part of his profits to the Receiver General under what is known as a business profits tax or a tax on incomes received from vessels. Do these ships belonging to the Government pay this business profits tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am afraid the hon. member will have to ask my colleague the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid). The railways are under the Minister of Railways, and the ships are also managed by Mr. Hanna and his Board of Directors. Just what taxes they pay, I do not know.

I move that the committee rise and report progress, so that we can get this information from the Minister of Railways.
Motion negatived.

The shipping question is one of very considerable importance to our part of the country. There is hardly a ton of soft coal that goes into the city of Montreal that does not come in one of our ships from Sydney. There is not a single ton of iron ore that goes into thAt city that does not cpme from Sydney or from our sister colony, Newfoundland, of which my hon. friend from Eunenburg is a native. I know rqy hon. friend is proud that from (he ancient colony of Newfoundland and from the furnaces in my county comes the cheapest iron that is produced in the world. I will not say steel, but I repeat, we can produce pig iron more cheaply than any other part of the world.
Now I want to pay a little attention to my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark). We have heard his theories so often. They
\

.are the theories that directed my little infantile legs from the cradle, but I have always found that a man who preached free trade was a protectionist in practice.
I wish I could pay my hon. friend the .compliment of saying that he was sincere both in theory and practice on either free trade or protection; but I fear I cannot do it. He was a supporter for fifteen years of a Government that preached free trade but practised protection. Is not that true?

The fifteen years began in 1896. I only came to Canada in 1902. My hon. friend surely won't hold me responsible for what happened in the six years before I came. I go one step further and point out fo my hon. friend that he ought to hold it as an extenuating circumstance, that the party got into thoroughly bad lines before I joined it, and I was misled by the name Liberal into thinking the party really was.

I am most pleased to receive my hon. friend's explanation. I invite him over. -We will give him a seat'here. Now for a moment we are going to lock horns seriously. My hon. friend would make it appear to this House that England became predominant in shipping during the days of free trade over there. Recalling the history I read when a boy, was it not in the-war between England and France when England captured Louisburg and became master of all the inland waters of Canada that England acquired her supremacy at sea, and from that time France's erstwhile predominance began to wane? As my hon. friend from West Peterboro (Mr. Burnham) pointed out this afternoon, the Americans said: We can make more money out of other business, so we 'will hire our ships from England. Let mp say this: It is within my own lifetime, and I am not the oldest man in this House, when the iron ore areas of Newfoundland were first discovered by Graham Fraser, the late president of the Nova Scotia Steel Company- a discovery which led to our beating the whole world, as we can to-day, at the smelting of ore from the coast of Newfoundland up there about Tilt Cove. We produce pig iron to-day more cheaply at Sydney harbour than in any part of this rotund globe. Coming now to free trade, it is a subject on which the people of Canada are fed up.
There are to-day in Canada over forty thousand miles of railroad and canals that have cost about.$150,000,000; and we take pride in our court houses, custom houses, post offices, and other public buildings. Did
any principle of free trade enter into their construction? Were they not rather built under thp aegis of a protective tariff. When hon. gentlemen who talk so much about free trade rise to speak in this House, I sometimes-if the decorum of this Chamber will countenance the expression-I sometimes admire their gall. I will ask these free traders this question:	Did they ever
know a single man in this House of Commons of Canada who was sincere enough in his convictions to assume the Premiership of this Dominion and put into force a free trade policy? No; they do not. I am going to follow my hon. friend from Red- Deer just a little further. Let me inform that hon. gentleman that I am not an Englishman; I am not an Irishman; I am not a Scotsman; I am a Canadian.
Hear, hear.

I repeat, I am a Canadian. And when I heard this afternoon the remarks of my hon. friend in regard to navigation and shipping I confess I was somewhat surprised- at the meagre extent of his knowledge of the subject. The British Isles, that were almost lost in the German ocean, were, he said, the centre of control and the seat of knowledge in regard to the science of shipping. Well, now, Mr. Chairman, Balboa, who found the route of the Panama Canal, was not a native of the British Isles, nor did -Columbus, the discoverer of America, have the honour to claim that spot as his home; and Cabot who explored the coast of North America was not, as far as I am aware, a native of the British Isles. I give Great Britain credit for beling the greatest colonizer that . the world has ever known, but she cannot be claimed to have been the greatest explorer. The man who wrecked the Empress of Ireland in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, I may say, hailed from those little islands in the German ocean. You never heard of a Nova Scotian ever having made such a mistake in navigation. Now I do not intend to pursue my hon. friend any further, for I see quite well that he works pn dreams and theories and not on practical knowledge. Let us get away from bickering and get down to solid facts.
A good idea.

Yes, certainly, a good idea; and as a matter of fact, let me say right now that there is in the county I represent a steel works that is capable of producing pig iron cheaper than any other city in the

world. This Government, and particularly the Minister of Marine, has entered into a contract with the company through which there has been establish'd a very large steel plate mill, the only ship plate mill in any place from the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic sea, with the exception of the " Smoky City " of the United States. We are able to produce them an ample supply of plates, as has been demonstrated within a very few weeks, and are likely to-be able to supply the entire Dominion as- well as a large portion of the United Kingdom, and may- possibly be called upon even by Pittsburgh for the supply of plates. This is something that was not dreamed of ten years ago. Ten years ago in my county people were wondering how it was possible for them to send coal up the St. Lawrence to compete with the coal mines of the United States. Previous to the election of 1911 the city of Montreal entered into a contract with a United States company for bituminous coal. They were to be supplied with 50,000 tons of coal for all the public works of Montreal at a price thirty-one cents below the tender of the Dominion Coal Company, and that notwithstanding the fact that fit that time the Dominion Coal Company and all Canadian coal companies had an advantage of fifty-four cents a ton. Under conditions of that kind it is rather difficult to understand why we people in the East of Canada are not a little bit prejudiced against the men in the West. We have very little in common with them. Do they buy our coal? When they bought our steel we gave it to them cheaper than they could buy it in England. We sent our steel rails around Cape Horn and sold them at a very cheap rate in Prince Rupert.
* These are facts. Now then, there is one other thing: I remember when I was a young fellow down in Nova Scotia the old men, and the old women too,-for I sometimes associated with the ladies-told me of the enormous cost of flour during the days of the Franco-Prussian war in 1870-1-2. They were paying $14 a barrel for flour. They thought it was, something enormous. This brings me back to my farmer friends down there who talk to us so very,'very much about profiteering. I am going to make this statement, that there is no class in this Dominion of Canada, that are greater profiteers than the farmers.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The only explanation
I can give is that owing to the very severe weather and the thickness of the ice it was quite impossible for the "Sealer" to reach the Magdalen Islands. Even the icebreaker " Montcalm" was stuck a month in the ice before she could reach the Magdalen Islands. We were using every endeavour within our power to get provisions to those
islands. We also tried to reach the islands with the "Sealer" but the ice was too thick. Eventually the, "Montcalm" got through.

It seems to me rather bad management on the part of the Canadian Alercantile Marine to have allowed a vessel -which I presume was not an icebreaker and therefore not fitted for a voyage in the depth of winter-to attempt such a trip. There is no doubt whatsoever that in so doing a great risk was being taken, and it seems to me that the Board of Management-should have obtained expert advice on the subject before sending a ship which was liable to be damaged on such a dangerous expedition. speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I wish at once to relieve the Canadian Alercantile Marine of the onus of sending the "Sealer" to the Magdalen Islands. The "Sealer" had not been turned over to the Canadian Government and it was my own department that forced her to go there. The people of the Magdalen Islands were on the verge of starvation; our icebreaker "Montcalm" was not available at that time; and the situation was so serious that the Government were considering the advisability of sending provisions by airship if they could not be conveyed in any other way. Therefore I think hon. gentlemen will agree that the Government were justified in taking the risk they did. I am glad to say the ship was not damaged, but it was our responsibility and our duty to load the. vessel with provisions and try to get her to the Alagdalen Islands if it was at all possible.

The other day we had the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) coming to this House and giving advice to the Government. speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
With regard to communication with the Magdalen Islands, 1 may say that the steamer " Lady Evelyn," owned by a private company and subsidized by the Government, was on that route, but, having become disabled about the month of November, was unable to continue her regular sailings. It would not be advisable for the Government to enter into competition with a private concern that was enjoying a subsidy from the Dominion Treasury, provided they were taking proper care of the passengers and freight, and I understand that they were. The " Lady Evelyn " will be repaired and again placed on that route, but if she is not able to carry on the -service I shall be very glad to bring the matter to the attention of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. The hon. member is quite right when he says that these ships are built primarily for the use of Canada and Canadians and that we must serve our home interests before, we serve our export interests abroad.
As to the other question raised by my hon. friend and also by the member for Westmorland (Mr. Copp), I have already given the information in answer to an inquiry made this afternoon by the member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archam-bault), but I shall be only too happy to give it again. I stated this afternoon that when the Government inaugurated their [DOT]shipbuilding programme,, early in 1918, the policy was to keep the Canadian steel shipbuilding yards fully occupied and to provide the tonnage that the Government desired to have. We did not call for public tenders because the business could not be handled in that way. One firm, for instance, in order to be glutted with business, might quote a price a shade lower than that quoted by another firm, and we would not have been able evenly to distribute the business. The greatest care, however, was exercised in obtaining prices from the different yards. :If we wanted a ship of 5,000 or 8,000 tons we asked the yards that were capable of turning out ships of that size what their prices were. We did not accept always the price that was quoted us; in many cases we carried on negotiations for weeks before the price was finally arranged that was satisfactory to the Government.
We had a check on the price through the experts in the Marine Department who figured out what the cost of a ship should be; and we had also the competitive bids from the various yards. Moreover, we knew what it would cost to build similar ships in the United Kingdom. If hon. members will ask the shipyards they will be told that we did not let them off very easily. In fact, the shipbuilders in British Columbia felt that their prices were being so much beaten down that they appealed to the members and did everything they could to get us to deal more liberally with them. But I and the officers associated with me did the best we could to get the very best prices. In comparison with what other countries have done, I do not think that we need be ashamed of the contract prices that were arrived at.

I endorse every word spoken by the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Parent) a few moments ago. It

The hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Parent) has just referred to the Magdalen islands and the coast of Gaspe. I would call the attention of the minister to the north shore of the St. Lawrence below' Quebec, the district which lies between Murray bay and Tadoussac, and as far as the Labrador coast. Last year I succeeded in obtaining from the minister the assurance that the steamer Champlain would be taken from her course and sent to ply between Murray bay and Tadoussac. This w'ent on very well for a certain number of months until last January, -when tenders were called for the sale of the boat. Recently, when I put a question in the House, the minister told me that there was no necessity for replacing the ship which was practically sold. I must protest against such an answer. There is a necessity for having a regular boat service from Murray bay down the river St. Lawrence all the time, and especially between the months of (October and May. I am told that there is a little story told about this ship, the Champlain. Tenders were called, a certain number of tenders w'ere reoeived, and one was accepted. The reason why the.sale was not proceeded with, I am informed, wras that some friends of the Government submitted a tender -which was to be accepted, but they could not finance the enterprise and pay for the ship. If we are going to -vote such a huge amount as $20,000,000 for ships, we should see to it that $500,000 or $600,000, or whatever may be necessary, is applied for building a boat to carry on the service, which is very necessary, along the coast between Murray bay and Tadoussac, and as far as Labrador.
There is another point. I was surprised this afternoon to hear the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol) defending the policy of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. This hon. gentleman, everybody knows, was connected for years past with a number of shipping companies, the Richelieu and Ontario, the Canada Steamship lines, and now he is one of the promoters of the Dominion Steamship Line, the Nova Scotia Steamship Line, and he is behind some of the big mergers that are going to be made of all the steel industries of this country, in. which English capital is interested. He is still a director of the

Dominion Steamships and the Canada Steamship Company, and a few weeks ago, just at the opening of this Parliament, I saw in the corridors no less a gentleman than Colonel Grant .Morden who was at the back of the merger of the Canada Steamship Line, -who, I am told, with Sir Newton Moore and other prominent men who came from Australia to this country especially for the purpose of organizing this huge steel .merger, came here to get an assurance from the minister and the Government that this would go through in order that their interests would be safeguarded. This is the story, and I know it because some people have told me so, and they are just as reliable people as the minister.
I would ask the Minister of Marine for a few moments to get away from those big amounts of money and see that the little affairs of his department are better at- . tended to. I am making no special charge, but I wish to draw to the attention of the minister that in the administration of his department there are many little details which were better looked after formerly, but which since this big policy of shipbuilding has been inaugurated, have been absolutely ignored. For instance,-while this may not be quite relevant to the question under discussion, I want to give an example.-the officers and employees of the steamer Champlain were to be given uniforms by the Minister of Marine, an amount was voted in the Estimates and the uniforms were to have been made. A few weeks ago I received some letters that the men have not yet got their uniforms. When we have the minister juggling with millions every day, the small details are not attended to, . and the poor people, the officers and other employees of the departments and also the people who live along the north shore of the river St. Lawrence, suffer.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The hail, member for Quebec W^st finds fault with this Government for having done nothing, as he says, for the city of Quebec. Let me say to him that since Sir Robert Borden formed his Government in 1911, we have spent from $25,000,000 to $30,000,000 on the city of Quebec, whereas in the fifteen years previous, when Sir Wilfrid La-urier was in power, less than $3,000,000 was spent on that city. So this Government has done pretty well, so far as the city of Quebec is concerned. My hon. friend who states that we have done nothing for the city of Quebec knows that we have built a 2,000,000-bushel elevator there; we have built the St. Malo shops, and have spent altogether some $25,000,000 on the city. We have made it at least equal to any other port so far as facilities are concerned. My Ivon, friend states that the city of Quebec is the terminal of the Transcontinental railway. I had always understood that Halifax and St. John were the terminals. I cannot for the life of me understand why somb hon. gentlemen opposite are so hostile to anything the Government may undertake for the purpose of putting the Canadian National Railway system in a position where it can compete with the great Canadian Pacific railway.
My hon. friend said that he had a right to criticise the administration of . Mr. Hanna. Of course he has that ri^ht. The only point I wish to make is ithat in justice to Mr. Hanna and the management of the system I hope the criticism will be fair and honest, and not made with the object of trying to injure the railway, or discouraging the management in such a way as to affect the operation of the system.
It seems to me that some hon. gentlemen opposite are trying to discourage the shipbuilding industry in this country. No one would regret it more than I, if by the- criticism that is being offered in this House, and which will go forth to the country, the shipbuilding industry in this country should [Mr. J. D. Reid 1
cease. It employs some 50,000 man, I believe.	[DOT]
Mr DUFF- About 23,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Well then, 23.000. The amount of money that is expended in wages in this industry is very large. Furthermore, every article that goes into the vessels that we are building is made in Canada from our natural resources. Even the ship pla-tes are made in this country. It seems to me that under a policy of this kind which keeps the money spent on the industry in this country, the shipbuilding industry, should be supported, and I for one am willing to do my part in encouraging the industry. Like other industries, it is for the advantage of Canada. The ships that we have built have done more to advertise Canada in certain countries, and to bring us trade, than has been done for many years past. Most of our .ships so far have been running to South America and the West Indies, with which formerly we had very little trade. They have brought \is closer together and have brought us trade, and will do more in that direction in the future. The same results will follow in other parts of the world when we get our shipbuilding programme completed. I for one urge upon every hon. member the vital importance of the national control of these ships in order that we may be able to compete with the great Canadian Pacific railway in the matter of freight charges on Canadian products, and be in a position to carry produce from the point of shipment to destination at cheaper rates than can be quoted by our great competitor. If we have vessels that can be operated in connection with our railways, with the advent of the time-which I do not believe is far distant-when we can make both ends meet in the working of the railway system,' we shall have solved the great problem of freight rates on the ocean, because we shall then be able to ship products from the place of production to its destination at probably a very much lower rate on the Atlantic than would be offered by our competitors if they had the practical control of the traffic from our Canadian ports.

I should not like the minister to leave the House under an impression which I am loath to characterize as intentionally incorrect. Last year when the Grand Trunk debate was on the minister, as a railway expert, vouchsafed his help to the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) who sometimes received that help with pleasure, and at other times, I venture to say, with mingled feelings. Last session the Minister of Railways often came into the House, as he has done tonight, with the avowed intention of throwing some light on the matter in order that we might understand it as perfectly as he thinks he understands it himself. He said repeatedly last year-and my memory is sound in this regard-that the section, of the Grand Trunk on American soil was highly important because it led to the port of Portland. This year, however, when we have tabled in this House the agreement between the Government and the Grand Trunk, the minister tells us that he has no
official knowledge of the proceedings taken by the Government in the* matter of expropriation. I can only say that if the minister desires to retain his reputation as a railway expert and be taken seriously by the people of the country and the members of ihis House, it is eminently desk-able that his speeches should be more studied. Proceedings are taken, the papers mention it, every member in the House is conversant with the subject, and people generally are aware of it; and the minister knows nothing about it he is the only person who is still in ignorance. This Government, which has diverted Canadian trade towards Portland, is composed of men who, when the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme was before the House, opposed it because they were not in favour of an altogether Canadian railway through Canada, but preferred at that time, as they prefer to-day, that only part of the railroad should be on Canadian soil; and they would rather give trade to -the Yankees than to Quebec. The minister says that the Borden Government did more .since the year 1911 for the province of Quebec than the Laurier Administration achieved during fifteen years. He mentioned the enormous sum of $25,000,000 spent in the city of Quebec. Now, how was that sum spent? Or, to be more precise, to be more in keeping with the methods generally adopted by this Government, 1 should ask, where was this money squandered? The Minister of Railways mentioned a grain elevator. I know that unfortunately, when he comes to our city, he remains only a few hours on his way to Saguenay, where he fishes trout or salmon; and the next time the hon. gentleman visits Quebec I invite him to call upon me and I shall be delighted to show him around the harbour. I will show him that- famous grain elevator of which he has boasted so profusely. The shell of the elevator is there, but it is empty. There is no grain in it, and there never was; and, if this Government is retained in power, there never will be.
My hon. friend also mentioned another bit of construction work on which he said millions had been spent, the workshops in St. Malo. Has the minister developed of late a sense of humour? Is it his desire to laugh at the population of Quebec and their representatives in this House? We know what the St. Malo workshops are to-day. They were to be the greatest workshops in Canada, according to the plans laid down by the Laurier Government. But this Government, so r far as those workshops are

concerned, has pursued the same policy it has followed in. connection with everything else, and that is to belittle the policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier thinking that it was given to small men to render as small as themselves a big statesman such as Sir Wilfrid Laurier was. The works are there, the minister can come on one of his trips to Quebec and we will their find if he has., any excuses to make about the millions spent in Quebec for building shops. Where were the millions spent? The millions were spent in Levis where the money was given to the friends of the Government to buy fields, property and lots so that the friends of the Government would make some money.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

I bow to your decision, Mr. Chairman. I think we have enough scandals in our own city without crossing the river and going over to Levis. I shall confine myself to Quebec. Millions, said the minister, have been spent in Quebec. A few months ago some western members came to our, city, and in company with several of my colleagues I took
10 p.m. the western members around the city and showed them what I thought were the points of interest. We came, on a street called St. Paul street, to a bam, a shed, a shack, half falling into ruins. I said: " That is the terminal station of the Canadian National railways in the city of Quebec/' I will show where the minister has spent other millions in the city of Quebec. Right under the Dufferin Terrace, to which thousands of visitors come every summer to admire the magnificent scenery of the St. Lawrence and the Laurentian mountains, at their very feet this 'Government has erected a building which is a disgrace, an eyesore to every one accustomed to view things which are not ugly. munificent Borden Government, which has spent millions of dollars according to the Minister of Railways. The city of Quebec gave them a magnificent property worth over flQ0,000 and in return this Government, to show their good faith, to show the interest they had in our city and district, erected a building worth about $25,000 which resembled more a match box than any railway station I ever looked at. Mr, CANNON: When the Minister of Rail ways spoke a moment ago his main argu ment was that ships are necessary to run our Canadian railways and that he wishes to have shipping lines as well as railway lines to compete with the Canadian Pacific. The policy of the Government, and especially the policy of the Minister of Railways, is in flagrant contradiction to the argument brought forward by him to-night

in the House of Commons at least as far as the city of Quebec is concerned. Establishing lines of railways to compete with the Canadian Pacific.
