speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. My hon. friend must remember that we are not here to discuss the treatment given to the city of Quebec by the present Government. We are discussing the shipbuilding programme of the Government. He must, according to the rule, remain strictly within the item of discussion.

Mr. Chairman, I do not
wish to discuss how badly Quebec has been treated but I wish to underline the remarks made by the minister as to the magnificent treatment given to Quebec by the Government. Now a shipping poliey is being considered. What will the, Government do for the city of Quebec as regards shipping?. Can we expect more in the future than we have had in the past? As I have said many times in this- House we have lots of confidence in the management of shipping under the very-able direction of the Minister of Marine. He does not claim, that he is a marine expert. as my hon. friend (Air. J. D. Reid) claims to be a railway expert. The Minister of Mai'ine is modest. He has not like the Minister of Railways been a minister for years. He has not yet forgotten his modesty. He has not, perhaps, ceased long enough to be a Liberal and has not become like the Minister of Railways a thorough Tory, and here let me say that I never met a thorough Tory who was modest, either in his person or in his demands.
I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Railways to one last point, and I hope that in doing so I will be in order. I do not think that he is much better acquainted with the Canadian Northern railway crowd than the Minister of Marine. The latter is starting a new experiment. I would ask 12
the Minister of Railways to be charitable enough to give pointers and information to our less informed Minister of Marine. The Minister of Railways has dealt with Alac-kenzie and Mann for over six years. He knows Mr. Hanna, he knows Sir Donald Mann, and he knows Sir William Mackenzie-in fact, I think he knows every prominent man in that crowd; the Minister of Marine does not. I will therefore ask the Minister of Railways to keep his own friends with him and not let that gang enter the office of the Minister of Alarine. Unfortunately the Minister of Railways told us that the Government had decided that in Canada's new policy it was imperative for the same men to run the trains as to run the ships. I say that this should not be. It is bad enough to have the old men of the Canadian Northern whom the ATinister of Railways knows so well, bad enough to have them again in harness running our Canadian railways to ruin, but this Government should see that the ships are protected from their clutches. Those ships were most unfortunate last fall. One was stranded at, the very spot where the Minister of Railways, after strenuous days of work, goes to take his rest fishing salmon, at the opening of the Saguenay river. There she lies, one of the first ships built by Canada, affording a very' sad spectacle. Another ship went further down the river and got caught in the ice, and she was experimenting to show the rest of the world that winter navigation was an easy task. A third ship disappeared on the coast of Nova Scotia, doubtless not having received instruction and advice from my hon. friend from Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Butts). This has been a poor start. The Minister of Marine ought now to change his policy and take control of matters into his own hands. For-those hands are very competent, the reputation that the Atinister of Marine has left in connection with the Harbour Commission of Alontreal is one of the best. Therefore he should take over the control of matters himself instead of having Alackenzie and Alann strand our ships after having wrecked railroads.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I wish to say a
word or two in reference to the port of Quebec. I concur almost altogether in what the hon. members from that famous city have said, with the exception of the statement of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, which was if I understood him correctly, that no grain had recently passed through the grain elevators at that port. Very large quantities of grain have passed through the elevators there. I am



not a pessimist as far as the port of Quebec is concerned. It is one of the best equipped ports in the North American continent; and now that the National Transcontinental railway is in running order not only the preseent government-owned ships but the larger ships that I hope will shortly be on the St. Lawrence route will make Quebec their terminus. I look forward to the port of Quebec doing a very much larger business than it has ever done in its past history for it is one of Canada's national ports and will be treated as such'. There is no warmer advocate of the further development of trade through the port of Quebec than I am; and I can assure hon. gentlemen personally, and also on behalf of the Government, that every thing will be done not only to make the port of Quebec what its parliamentary representatives quite properly desire it to be, but what the situation of Quebec and the facilities which it possesses should render it-a port doing fifty or one hundred times more business than it is doing at the present time. I for one am satisfied that more freight is going to pass through Quebec and more siiips are going to stop there. Naturally, owing to the existing depth of water large ships stop there at present and the larger vessels that are to come will also do so. I hope that a year from now, if we are spared. I will be able to show hon. gentlemen that the business of the port of Quebec has grown and has exceeded in volume anything it has ever done in the past.
Where does Three Rivers come in?

We are all pleased with the speech which the Minister of Railways gave us this evening, although I do not know whether 1 should apologize for bringing him in, or thank him for coming. The minister may know a great deal about railways but he has certainly shown by his speech tonight that he knows nothing about shipping; and when any member of the Government tells this committee that we cannot run railways without ships I think he had better go away back and sit down, and learn. If the operation of ships and railways is to form part of the Government's policy why should the Government not operate farms also? Why should it not go into the West, cultivate a couple of million acres, and produce stuff for this great railway that he talks about to carry to the seaboard to be there placed on steamships and transported across the ocean? The minister rather insinuated, if I might be allowed to use the expression, that if the Canadian Mercantile Marine was

not built and operated so as to convey across the ocean the products to be carried by the Canadian National railways from the West the Canadian Pacific railway would gobble up the business. Of course, that is the old game,-trying to make out that we are in favour of the Canadian Pacific and against the nationalization or public ownership of railways. But that argument does not go-very far, because it will be a long time before the tramp steamers that the Government are building will compete with the steamers of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. It is useless for (the minister to draw a comparison between the Canadian Pacific steamers which carry goods brought from the West to Montreal and St. John on the Canadian Pacific railway and the Canadian Government steamers which take goodjs from Montreal, Quebec, St. John, or Halifax, because the two classes of steamers are quite different. The buyer in Liverpool or in Lop-don knows exactly when the Canadian Pacific steamers will arrive, but the tramp steamers cannot operate on any specific schedule; consequently the shippers will not send on the tramp steamers the same class of goods that they will send on steamers that carry both passengers and freight.
The /Minister of Railways knows so much about shipping that he has told us that through the construction and operation of these ships a great deal of business had been opened up between Canada and South America and the West Indies. But that is not the case, because this business was opened up long before the Canadian Government built and operated these ships, and although I am not a prophet or the son of a prophet, I venture the assertion that that trade will be there when within five years from now the Canadian Government shipq are scrapped and sold as old junk.
But -what aroused the anger of the Minister of Railways was my simple question whether the business profits' tax would be paid by the company operating these steamers. The minister rather sidestepped the question by saying, in the first place, that these steamers had not been operated for a year. Of course, I have to take the-minister's word, but my memory is fairly good, and I think he will not deny that some of these vessels have been operating for nearly two years. Now is the time-when every business man must file a statement with the Inspector of Taxation concerning his business profits. What I want to know is whether this marine company is filing a statement similar to that which

every private shipbuilding company has to file. Just here I would like the Minister of Marine to answer two questions that I put to him this afternoon. First, how much of the $1,400,000 which he says was the profit in connection with the operation of nineteen ships, was placed to rest account for depreciation?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I explained this afternoon that the profit statement had been arrived at after providing for depreciation, interest on the cost of the ship, insurance, overhead charges and operating expenses. The amount allowed for depreciation is, I understand, five per cent. The hon. member will agree that that is a fair amount to allow for depreciation on a new ship. I repeat the statement I made this afternoon that none of these nineteen ships have been in commission a year. Some of them have made only one voyage; others have made only two.

Then, there was the question of sterling exchange. With regard to the difference between the cost of vessels here and the cost in England, was sterling exchange figured on the basis of $4.86, or at the current rate?
Mr. BAflXiANTYNE:' At $4.86.

Then the minister did not give the House proper information this afternoon when he made a comparison between the cost of vessels in Canada and the cost of vessels in England, because everybody knows that six months ago English sterling was quoted at' only $3.60.
He would have to make a new estimate every week.

I thank my hon. friend for that suggestion. But the price per ton should be figured either at the average rate or at the highest rate, whichever the minister likes. It was not fair to make a comparison based on a rate of $4.86 for the pound sterling.
Mr. BAjLiLANTYNE : It really does not .make very much difference, because during the past two years the cost of some types of ships has been about the same in the yards of the United Kingdom as in the Canadian yards. The point I tried to make was that during the past two years ships could be built as cheaply in the yards of Canada as in the yards of the United Kingdom.	,

That does not alter the fact that if a man wanted to buy a ship in the British Isles he would pay for it at the
42J
prevailing rate of exchange; consequently, as I say, it was not fair for the minister to base his comparison upon a rate of $4.86 for the pound sterling.
The minister has kindly told me that the amount put to rest account for depreciation on these ships is five per cent. For the sake of argument we will say that that is a fair amount,,but these ships are new, and during the first year new ships require hardly any repairs. The minister will find out before he is a manager of ships very long -I beg his pardon; he transfers them to his friend the Minister of Railways-the Minister of Railways will find out that five per Cent will not go far for depreciation.
It has been stated that nineteen ships earned $1,400,000; that is about $73,000 per ship. Well, the Minister of Marine has no occasion to congratulate himself upon a vessel of 4,000 or 5,000 tons earning only ,$73,000. That is a mere bagatelle, and tl^e only reason why they earned that is because of the present abnormal conditions-conditions which will not be prevailing in the years to come. If they could earn only $73,000 with freight rates as they are to-day, they will earn practically nothing when the freight rates are reduced. Then, from the $73,000 has not been deducted the business profits tax which the ordinary shipbuilding company has to pay. Next year the net profit will ibe reduced a good deal by the .payment of this tax.
I am opposed to the Government operation of ships, because it is not fair to private companies or private interests'. It will discourage the building of 'ships by private interests. There is no reason why the (Government should enter upon a shipbuilding programme now that the war is over. The minister says that if they have not the ships he/cannot carry liis goods after they arrive at the seaboard. Well, how many railways in the United States have steamship lines? Perhaps one or two, but most of them have no steamships; they go out in the open market and make arrangements for the carrying of their freight, and that is what, this Government could do. It is not necessary that the Minister of Railways should have ships to carry the freight which comes over his line from Winnipeg or other western points to ports on the Atlantic ocean. Moreover, in the next year or two when freight rates reach a normal figure, the Minister of Marine and the Minister of Railways and the Government will find that instead of making $73,000, they will lose that much and a lot more. In addition to that, the property is decreasfiGO

in" in value and it will cost a great deal more to keep it in repair. The Government, therefore, will find that instead of having a bonanza as thejr think they have, they will have a white elephant on their hands.

If the Minister of Marine
sent a hurried message out to have his colleague the Minister of Railways come in and help him through with this, item, I am afraid he- made a mistake in doing so, because the Minister of Railways has put before the Committee arguments that must be answered. I suppose the Minister of Railways was hurriedly aroused from his afterdinner rest and came into the House somewhat ^excited, and he possibly went a little further than die would otherwise have gone. But he having gone so far, we .must find out just what this means, and we are getting some information, even if we are getting it piecemeal and through somebody getting rather excited and saying things that possibly he would not otherwise have said. The Minister of Railways says tonight that we must oontinue in this shipbuilding programme because we cannot successfully operate 22,000 miles of railway unless we have nineteen ships to help us do so. When I asked him if the 22,000 miles of railway included the Grand Trunk Railway system that was to be taken over under the Act which was passed at the last session of Parliament and under an agreement that lias already been entered into between the Government of Canada and the Grand Trunk Railway Company, he said it did. Then, this only loads up that system with $75,000,000 over and above the $700,000,000 or $800,000,000 of ,a burden which the people #f Canada were obliged to shoulder under the legislation passed last session. My hon. friend says that he as Minister of Railways is going to see to it that not one pound of freight that is brought from the West down to the city of Montreal is going io find an outlet through .any other ports than our own Canadian ports. How does ho get past the statement which he has made many times in this House, namely, that he as Minister of Railways or the Gov-cinment has nothing whatever to do now with the operation of the Canadian National railways; that that system is in the hands of a Board of Management, land the Government is absolutely cut clear and loose from any interference with the operation of that railway? That is what we were tojd last year. I want to ask the minister this question. When that load of wheat that he,
{Mr. Duff.]
with his fertile imagination, loaded up in the great West a few moments ago, is brought down over the Canadian National railways' to the city of Montreal, if Mr. Hanna, or the Board of Management that has charge of the Canadian National railways, gives an order to take that load to Portland, will my Iron, friend interfere and have it sent down to St. John or Halifax to be shipped from there? Can my hom friend do that under the arrangement he has today with this Board of Management of the Canadian National railways?
So much for wlhat the Minister of Railways has said. I want to ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballan-tyne) a question. I believe he said that there were seventeen different shipbuilding plants in the Dominion of Canada -with which he had entered into arrangements for the building of vessels. I want to ask him if the Government have in any way assisted in the construction of these plants for the different companies who are building these ships.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In no way whatever.

I w'ant to draw the attention of the Committee to the fact that we have from the Minister of Marine this afternoon and evening the information that he has given contracts for the building of 63 vessels of different tonnage and types to seventeen different companies. I want to protest in the strongest manner possible that it is not reasonable to expect that we shall get the best possible solution of the difficulties that arise in giving out contracts by one man being able to go to seventeen different contracting firms in the Dominion of Canada and say to them: I want you to build me so many vessels. I give my hon. friend all credit for doing the very best he can and getting the best prices he can from these firms. But it is not natural for water to run up hill; and it is not natural and not a proper business method for my hon. friend to go to the different shipbuilding firms in the Dominion and ask them what they will build a vessel for. The only safe and reasonable way to carry out the construction of these vessels for which we are to-night asking the people of Canada to Shoulder a burden of $20,000,000, is for tenders to be called for, and then company "A" does not know what company "B" is going to tender, and company "B" does not know what company "C" is going to tender, and so on down all the line of the seventeen different companies. Instead of that,

contracts are being entered into behind closed doors without the people of Canada having any opportunity of expressing an opinion, without any tenders having 'been asked, without any person but the seventeen different companies knowing that any such contracts were to be let. My hon. friend lets'these contracts; he comes back *to the Cabinet Council and he makes a recommendation that a certain contract be let to a certain individual company, and an Order in Council is passed. That is all the people of Canada have 'to say about this expenditure of $75,000,000 for the purpose of building ships without which the Minister of Railways says he cannot successfully operate 22,000 miles of railway, part of which is a bankrupt railway that he is taking out of the hands of individuals and companies in which some of our friends in different parts of the Dominion of Canada are deeply interested.

not his prejudice, legitimate prejudices perhaps, against the city and port of Quebec carry him away to such an extent that he will not put into practise his more practical views, let not his reason be overwhelmed by what might be termed his political emotions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am sure my hon. friend is aware that public tenders are as a rule called for, and quite properly so, but we could not follow that policy in ordering ships. For argument's sake, suppose I had called for public tenders for six ships of 8,400 tons. Suppose that the Vickers Company, of Montreal, and five or six other shipbuilders had tendered, and that the Davie Shipbuilding Company, of Lauzon, which has not the facilities for turning out that number of ships except after a very long time, were the lowest tenderers. The Government would have no option but to award them the contract. We would not be able to distribute the orders. I quite understand the point of the leader of the (Opposition, and that is, the desirability of safeguarding the public interest. The statute from which he has quoted makes it plain that the minister has power to use his best judgment, and the Government to purchase by the best means what it requires. I do not know of any method that would so well safeguard the public interest as the course we have followed. I believe we got lower prices than we should have obtained by public tender. When the Government asked for prices on ships, as I have already twice stated to-day, they did not necessarily take the prices that were quoted. If a price was considered satisfactory it was accepted and if it was too high it was of course refused. By the method we followed we were in a position to distribute the business evenly over seventeen yards at a cost probably lower than if we had called for public tenders in the way suggested by the leader of the Opposition. It must be borne in mind also that time is an important feature of the programme, and we could not allow one yard to take more business than it was capable of turning out. |Some yards have two berths, some four and some six, and all these facts have to be taken into consideration in allotting the wrork. It was desirable to distribute the contracts in such a way that labour would not be concentrated in one particular place, but that workers would be evenly employed throughout the seventeen yards from Halifax to Prince Rupert. I have already said that the Government are at an end of their steel

programme, and if I thought that the suggestion of the leader of the Opposition, whose opinion I regard very highly, was of any practical importance I would gladly recommend it to the Government. But from the business experience that I have gained during the last thirty or thirty-five years, I am bound to say that I think the Government have followed the best possible course.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: With all deference to the minister, I would point out that what I quote from the statute is part of the law of the land.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It gives the minister an option.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There may be reasons of expediency of one kind or another why it should be advisable to allow the minister to distribute work from the Atlantic to the Pacific and allot it to different shipyards; but this Parliament has certainly laid it down in black and white that, in the matter of public contracts, where the amount exceeds $5,000 there shall be no option on the part of the minister. The minister says that the statute gives him the right to do as he thinks best. Let me once again quote the section:
Whenever any works are to be executed under the direction of any department of the Government, the minister having charge of such department shall Invite tenders by public advertisement for the execution of such works.
That is the law. There are certain exceptions. The minister referred to subsection three, which provides that where the estimated cost of the work is less than $5,000 and it appears to the minister, in view of the nature of the work, that it is not advisable to invite tenders-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister
says " That is it." He will note, however, that this sub-section applies only to works under $5,000. But the contracts under consideration vary in amounts from half a million to two million dollars apiece. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) is in his place and I am quite prepared to leave it to him to say as to whether or not my interpretation of the statute is not literally correct, namely, that the law provides that where a contract is of an amount over $5,000 there shall not be, except under certain specified circumstances, any option to the minister to distribute the work as he likes. He is obliged to call for tenders by public advertisement.
Are there not two qualifying subsections?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Yes; first,
subsection "A" which provides against any pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest. When speaking before, I pointed out that possibly these contracts v^ere awarded in war-tin e, when there was a pressing emergency.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Most of them.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister, however, is inclined to base his right in the matter on a section which, I am afraid, cives him no ground whatever to stand on .

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Most of these contracts were entered into under the' War Measures Act, but even if they were not made under that Act, and putting aside altogether the legal aspect of the argument,
1 think that any business man in this House will agree with me that it would be unwise to attempt to order ships under public tender by leason of the wide distribution of the yards. Some of these yards are large and some small, and it Was the desire of the Government not only to get the ships as quickly as possible but to have the labour distributed evenly throughout the country.
Will the leader of the Opposition be good enough to read section "B."?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I will read the entire clause:
Whenever any works are to be executed under the direction of any department of the Government, the minister having charge of such department shall invite tenders by public advertisement for the execution of such works, except in cases
(a)	of pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest; or
(b)	in which, from the nature of the work, it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by officers and servants of the department ; or
(c)	where the estimated cost of the work Is less than $5,000, and it appears to the minister, in view of the nature of the work, that it is not advisable to invite tenders.
I contend that a point of order could be raised in this connection, and would be sustained if it were raised. I do not raise it. however, because I have no wish in any way to delay the programme that the Government has under way. I believe it was started in a period of war. These contracts have already been awarded, and to raise a point at this stage would only be to delay the final execution of the work. But I do say that we should have from the Government, before allowing this item to pass, a declaration as to future contracts. The ground the minister has taken at present I do not think we can permit to stand for a

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think it is quite clear that without getting outside of the terms of the law, what -was done was perfectly justifiable. What was pressing to get done was precisely to get the whole Shipbuilding capacity of this country at work, and this end could not be attained if you called for tenders and proceeded to allot the work to the lowest tenderer. It was probably as important to get the shipyards all to work, as it was to get the ships themselves.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is the minister speaking in reference to the war period?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
What is being done
now is merely completing what was started during the war. As to a declaration of future action, there is no doubt that the Government intends that, when the exceptional circumstances that prevail in the present instance do not apply, they will be governed by the law as it stands, so long as that law remains on the statute book. But I think that a moment's reflection will show that the condition here comes very well within the first clause which gives the minister an option in cases of pressing necessity. It must be quite clear that if we gave all the work to the lowest tenderer we would experience considerable delay in getting the ships; and super-added to this fact, there was the desirability, apart altogether from the necessity for the ships; of providing work for the entire shipbuilding facilities of Canada. When you say that you should call for tenders from all the shipbuilding plants of Canada, in the nature of things you could not do this particular thing in that particular way. You could not get the result. You could not get the ships which we were pressing to get promptly and as early as possible. If you called for tenders, gave the contracts to the lowest tenderers and waited until the lowest tenderers could get the ships finished you would be waiting still.	[DOT]

I listened with a great deal of interest to the explanation given by the hon. the Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne) as to why he did not ask for tenders, and I was not convinced by what
fMr. Mackenzie King.]
lie told us. From a purely business standpoint it was proper to advertise. We do not expect one shipyard is going to build all the ships required by'"the country, but surely the hon. gentleman could ask for tenders and limit the time that any one tenderer might have to build a ship. The practice of allowing a minister or a Government to spend $75,000,000 of the people's money by arrangement with shipbuilding companies and deciding how these contracts shall be distributed from Halifax to Vancouver is wrong. It is not in the interest of the people that this should be done and it is not the proper way to carry on .public business. I listened very attentively to the minister this afternoon and I regret very much that we did not have the pleasure of hearing his answer to the question put by my hon. friend from Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) this evening. My hon. friend asked: Where is the $20,000,000 to come from? He was ruled out of order by the Chairman on the ground that this is not a matter to be taken up at this time. It seems to me that it is good business to find out before you arrange to spend your money where it is coming from. I think that is what the people want to know. I believe the statement by the hon. gentleman showed that we were making money out of the steamship business but I think he will agree with me that conditions are abnormal. He cannot expect that freights will continue where they are to-day. He knows, and nobody knows better than he, that it is only a matter of a short time, until freights will decrease in volume; there will not be so many cargoes to carry, some of the ships -will probably have difficulty in securing business, and we will consequently operate at a loss.
I notice that there have been a great many recommendations in the press recently as to the desirability of establishing a shipbuilding business in Canada. When I read these articles in the newspapers I sometimes wonder where they emanate from, and I am not quite sure that this insistent demand that the Government shall keep on shipbuilding does not emanate from the gentlemen who are profiting out of it I am not quite, sure that they are not behind the movement to create a public sentiment in support of shipbuilding. Might I suggest to my hon. friend that those people who have made so much money out of building ships when the war was on should continue the business without asking the Government to guarantee their profit now the war is over. What they are doing is what the railway builders did in the past. Contractors built railways, made their profit, but when the profits

dwindled and deficits occurred they handed these railways over to the Government and put the burden on the shoulders of the people. These people who are in the shipbuilding business have been making their profits and they desire to continue (Making profits but they want to hand the business of operating over to the people so that the people will pay the deficit on- operations.
_ The important question in connection with this matter is, I repeat, that which was asked by my hon. friend from Pontiac. It is true that the question should be discussed on the Budget but I believe that the Minister of Finance will have enough to do to handle the finances of this country without putting the people into a business that is going to lose them money. It is not good business and the people insist that this Government should carry on their affairs with reasonable business caution. It is not good business to ask the people to invest $20,000,000 when we are told that the shipbuilding business will have to be subsidized. The hon. the Minister o,f Marine would not put his own money into a prospect if he thought that it would be unsuccessful with a possible loss within a few years; and if that is the case why should he put the money of the people into this enterprise now? I listened to his remarks withrefer-ence to the cost and I was very much impressed with his statement that we were building ships at a reasonable price in Canada to-day. We were told that we were building ships at approximately $160 per deadweight ton. But the hon. gentleman knows full well that we wall have to compete in a short time with ships that were built in pre-war days at from $60 to $70 a ton. There is only one way to meet that competition and that is to take the loss because lower freights will get the business. As against what we are doing here, the United States Government are selling -their ships and I am told that they are so anxious to get out of the business that they are willing to sell them at $100 a ton. At the very time that they are willing to take a loss and go out of the business we are going into the business, putting $20,000,000 more of the people's1 money into it and, then we are told that we will have to subsidize it very shortly. On top of that we are told that $75,000,000 of the people's money is spent without a single tender being asked for. It is all right for hon. gentlemen to spend their own money if they want to, but they 11 p.m. are the trustees of the public and they have no right to spend the people's money without giving^ the
people the protection of public tenders and full knowledge as to whom these contracts have been awarded and why.
There is also the question of where these ships are going and what freights they are to carry. The hon. gentleman told us today that one of these steamers had left Vancouver for Australia. He did not tell us what she was bringing back from Australia. I think we know pretty well just what they export from Australia. They export wool, hides, wheat and tallow. They will not bring that kind of a cargo back to Canada. They will probably go to England and from England they will get a cargo to bring back here. There is no objection to that; if we are in the carrying trade that is good business. But why should we spend cur money to establish and operate a line to build up business between Australia and England? It is not good business. We were also told that these ships would carry cargoes to South America. What do they carry from South America?-cattle, grain and hides. These they take to the English market. This is all right for Great Britain, a great food-consuming country. They send out their finished products, bring back raw materials and get cargoes both ways. We do not want any wheat in this country, we are not looking for cattle, we are not asking for mutton; and yet these are the things that are being carried from Australia and the Argentine to England. The conditions in Canada do not parallel those of Great Britain, consequently there is not the same possibility of a mercantile marine being a financial success. These, amongst others, are the reasons why I am opposed to this vote and I shall oppose it here and shall also oppose it when we come to its consideration in the Budget.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I think we ought to clear up this point in regard to future contracts. I am sorry that the Prime Minister, or the Acting Prime Minister, is not here to speak but possibly the Minister of Justice could make a statement on behalf of the Government as to whether in regard to future contracts the Government will adopt the policy of calling for tenders as required by statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Government contemplates in future abiding by the provisions of the law as it understands it has abided by the provisions of the law in the past. If the circumstances which seem to have existed in this case, and which made it necessary and justifiable under the provisions of the statute to take the course we

did, arise again, I am not in a position to say that the same thing would not be done. But the Government, as I understand, will apply and conform to the general rule of the law save where the circumstances set forth in the law as justifying an exception shall arise.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Would the minister say whether he thinks that this particular expenditure would be justified under the exception with reference to inviting tenders provided for by subsection (c) which says:
Where the estimated cost of a work is less than $5,000 and it appears to the minister, in view of the nature of the work, that it is not advisable to invite tenders.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not prepared to
say the cost of the work should be under $5,000. The first subsection, if I remember correctly, does amply cover the particular case here where there was the necessity of getting ships in the shortest possible time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The Minister of Justice takes a view quite different from the view of the Minister of Marine as to his rights under this particular section.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the leader of the Opposition will allow me. My view is exactly the same as that of my colleague; you have got to take all the sections together.

I do not know whether as a layman I am not justified in putting forward my view here where so many lawyers are talking. It strikes me that the law as quoted by the leader of the Opposition covers this case exactly although not in section C nor perhaps in section A. - If I understood the Minister of Marine correctly he gave us to understand that these vessels were more expeditiously and economically constructed under the plan adopted by the Government than they covild have been' under any other plan. If I am correctly repeating what I understand the minister to say then you have the reason given in section B.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No.
I think so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My hon. friend has not observed that section (B) states " more economically or expeditiously executed by ofii-cers of the department." This work has been done by shipbuilding companies. I will read my hon. friend the section so that he will see the point for himself:

in which from the nature of the work it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department.
I think that answers my hon. friend's point. This work has not been done by officers of the department, it has been done by contractors.
Carried.
This item should certainly not carry-
Oh, oh.

-and the. more so in view of the refusal of the members of this Government to accede to the most reasonable suggestion of the leader of the Opposition that in future they would interpret the law as. demanding that in connection with the proposed expenditure of $20,000,000 of the people's money the law should be applied as in ordinary cases. The war is over and it is of paramount necessity that the Government of Canada should realize it. They were given during the war very wide powers. Let me tell them, with all respect, that, the people of Canada, and His Majesty's loyal Opposition as representing a large proportion of those people, do not propose that they should be allowed to carry on as they were allowed to do during the war. The law is absolutely plain. The Minister of Justice nods his head with confirmatory action. I am, Mr. Chairman, specially qualified to speak upon this question because when a law student I sat not at the feet of Gamaliel but at the feet of the Minister of Justice. Now let me read section 36:
Whenever any works are to be executed under the direction of any department of. the Government, the minister having charge of such department shall invite tenders by public advertisement for the execution of such works-[DOT]
That is the general principle. Here are the three exceptions:
Except in cases-
(a) of pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest.
Now the war being over how can any one pretend that there is a pressing emergency which would enable the Government of this country to over-ride the principle of the law. There is no such pressing emergency.

How do you know?
You have got to back that up with more than your statement. Your statement is not sufficient. '

For this .reason: We and the LTnited States are the two great

nations of this continent. Our economic life, our industrial development, and our trade relationships with the rest of the world are very much on a parity. The United States instead of going ahead with their shipbuilding programme are selling the ships which they built during the war. That is one good reason. Now a "pressing emergency" is one in which delay would be injurious to the public interest-not to private interest- not to the interest of one yard as opposed to another yard but to the interest of the whole public of Canada. I do not believe that any member who supports this Government, if he were, talking to me quietly outside of the House, would contend that there was any such pressing emergency at this time requiring the immediate construction of ships in this country and that this protection of the public interest-this protection to safe and sound and honest business-should be disregarded. Now what is the next exception?

May I ask my hon.
friend a question?
I would be delighted.

That may be. Is it not true that after an agreement was entered into by which wheat and flour passed freely between, Canada and the United States, the latter country saw fit to place an embargo on Canadian wheat going into that country? That is true, I think I am stating the facts correctly. I think one reason why the United States did that was because they wanted to make sure that they could secure the necessary ships to get their own wheat out of the country, and so they prevented Canadian wheat entering the United [DOT]States, and going to their own ports and probably taking up the shipping space that would be required to ship their own wheat. If that is true I do not think we should be placed in the position of depending upon the United States or any other country for ships; we ought to have ships to transport our own goods. There you see the public interest, and not a private interest. It is the interest of all those who have goods to ship.

In answer to what has been rather a "shorter catechism" than a question by the hon. gentleman, I would say that you cannot regard a condition as a pressing emergency when there is a very serious difference of opinion in the country as to whether the Government's programme is a wise or unwise one. The words "pressing emergency" must mean an emergency
which is so pressing that there can be no practical difference of opinion among the people of the country as to the necessity. For instance, when war breaks out, if it is neeesarv to build a ship or construct a bridge-

Or repair a wharf.
Mr. McMASTER-or repair a wharf, something of that kind, the minister in charge would be able to do it. There you would have a presing emergency; we can all imagine many instances of that kind. But here is the continuation of a shipbuilding programme which has been going on for several years and which I cannot regard as being a "pressing emergency " in any way, shape or manner. >
The second exception to the general rule to which I invite attention is:
(b) in which from the nature of the work it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department.
That exception does not apply. The third exception is:
Where the estimated cost of the work is less than $5,000 and it appears to the minister in view of the nature of the work that it is not advisable to invite tenders.
In order to come within this third exception the estimated cost of the work must be less than $5,000 and it must be the opinion of the minister that it would not be wise to ask for tenders. Certainly these exceptions do not apply; therefore the only ground that the minister has to stand on is the view that a pressing emergency exists and that to fail to act as he proposes would be injurious to the public interest. Now, believing sincerely that this policy is a mistake and that the Government is not a proper agency for the operation of tramp steamers, I think that the public interest would be better served by the abandonment of the scheme. But certainly there is no such emergency as would take this matter out of the plain principle of the law, a principle which every man administering the ihoney of others must desire to adhere to, namely, that he shall openly ask for tenders for anything that he has to buy or any work that he wishes t'o be performed in order that he may be able to say to those whoSe money he is administering: If it costs more than you thought it should cost, the fault is not mine: I gave full notice to every one and that is the lowest price at which after public tender and public ad-rertisement I could get the work done. Mr. BAl^LANTYNE: If the hon. member would allow me, perhaps we might save a little time. I am, of course, not responsible for what any publisher might print, but apparently he has given the list of ships that have been contracted for by the Government along with the ships that are in commission. Does that mean, therefore, that some ships have been contracted for that are to be paid for out of this vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not at all.
Then the amount of $63,000,000 is wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am not accountable for a newspaper article.
Air. AleMASTER: I know that.
Air. A1ACKENZIE KING:	This amount
of $20,000,000, that we are being asked to vote is a very large sum; we have been discussing this item a long time, and I think there has been no effort on this side to obstruct, but only to elicit such information as is in the public interest. I should like to ask the minister to let the item stand for discussion at some subsequent sitting of the House. It is a large enough sum to warrant further discussion, and we ought perhaps to have a little more information as to just what the consequence would be of the item not carrying. I should like to hear from the minister just how far the programme he has in view is from completion and in what degree it would be affected if the item should not carry.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the item did not carry, of course, that would be the end ol it. While I would like very much to meet the views of the leader of the Opposition, because the Government has been met in a very fair spirit, not only by himself but by all the members opposite,-and I might say that this is not the first occasion on which they have treated this question as a national one, but they have done so at previous sessions-I gave to the best of my ability very detailed information this afternoon; we have been on this item now since half past three o'clock. Much as I should like to meet the views of the Opposition, I think we ought really to pass the item now. If there is any further information that- the leader of the Opposition or any other hon. member desires, I should be glad to give it, but we are all anxious to get through with the business of the session.

This is a very important item amounting to $20,000,000, one of the largest items that is submitted for our consideration. Undoubtedly, a number of hon. members who have not been present in the House this afternoon and evening may require some further information. I am sure that on this side of the House we do not want to obstruct this item in any way, but merely wish to elicit the information we require in order to justify this expenditure. The Government, therefore, should not refuse postponing until a further date the consideration of the item.
